record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in Polyomino Tilings
record.original_question: Let a polyomino be a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares on the square lattice. If a polyomino tiles the plane using only translated copies and copies rotated by 180 degrees, must it also have a tiling of that same translated-and-180-degree-rotated type that is isohedral, meaning that any two tiles are related by a symmetry of the tiling?

evidence.quote: Definitions. A polyomino is a subset of R2 formed by a strongly connected union of axis-aligned unit squares centered at locations on the square lattice Z2.
If a tiling T has the property that for all Ti, Tj∈ T , there exists a symmetry of T mapping Ti to Tj, then T is isohedral; otherwise the tiling is non-isohedral

it is unknown if this is true for tilings using other subsets of the eight possible orientations. Specifically, isohedral tilings using only translated and 180◦-rotated copies of the prototile are characterized by those polyominoes satisfying Conway’s criterion
Open Problem 2 (Open Problem 3 of [27]) Does every polyomino that has a tiling using only translated and 180◦-rotated copies also have such a tiling that is isohedral?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work in the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2$. A polyomino is a subset of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that is a strongly connected (i.e., interior-connected) finite union of axis-aligned closed unit squares centered at points of $\mathbb{Z}^2$. A tiling of the plane by a prototile $P$ is a collection $T = \{T_i\}_{i \in I}$ of congruent copies of $P$ whose interiors are pairwise disjoint and whose union is $\mathbb{R}^2$. Such a tiling is said to use only translated and $180^\circ$-rotated copies if every tile $T_i$ is obtained from $P$ by either a pure translation or a translation composed with a rotation by $180^\circ$. A tiling $T$ is isohedral if for every pair of tiles $T_i, T_j \in T$ there exists an isometry of $\mathbb{R}^2$ that maps $T$ onto itself (i.e., a symmetry of $T$) and sends $T_i$ to $T_j$.

Question: Does every polyomino $P$ that admits some tiling of the plane using only translated and $180^\circ$-rotated copies of itself also admit such a tiling (using only translated and $180^\circ$-rotated copies) that is isohedral?
artifact.status_search_result: The problem appears to remain open. It is restated as an open problem in the polyomino tiling literature, and known polynomial-time algorithms decide isohedral tileability under such symmetry sets (characterized via Conway's criterion), but no published resolution of whether translation-and-half-turn tileability implies isohedral translation-and-half-turn tileability was found.

status_evidence.title: A Quasilinear-Time Algorithm for Tiling the Plane Isohedrally with a Polyomino
status_evidence.snippet: Isohedral tilings using only translated and 180°-rotated copies of the prototile are characterized by polyominoes satisfying Conway's criterion.
status_evidence.claim: Characterization of isohedral half-turn tilings is via Conway's criterion, but the question of whether tileability by half-turns implies isohedral tileability is posed as an open problem.

status_evidence.title: Isohedral Polyomino Tiling of the Plane
status_evidence.snippet: A plane tiling is isohedral if the symmetry group of the tiling acts transitively on the tiles.
status_evidence.claim: Standard reference defines isohedrality; does not report resolution of the half-turn open problem.
